title: The Warning Sign People Stopped Seeing
passage:
A coastal town had placed large tsunami evacuation signs along its waterfront after a major safety review. The signs used bright colors, arrows, and clear maps showing routes to higher ground. For the first year, residents often mentioned them and visitors stopped to read them. Five years later, an emergency drill revealed an unexpected problem. Most residents knew the general direction of higher ground, but many could not remember the nearest designated evacuation point.

Town officials first assumed that the signs had become faded or damaged. An inspection found the opposite. The signs were clean and readable. Some had recently been replaced. A disaster-prevention specialist suggested that physical visibility and psychological attention were different. People who passed the same sign every day might stop actively processing it, just as commuters may stop noticing familiar advertisements.

The town tested this idea during the next drill. Volunteers interviewed participants immediately after they walked past evacuation signs. Nearly everyone remembered seeing a sign somewhere along the route, but fewer could describe its map or the name of the evacuation site. Visitors who had arrived in town that week often remembered more details than long-term residents. Familiarity seemed to reduce attention.

Replacing signs every year with new designs would be costly and could create confusion. Instead, officials added smaller changing panels beneath the permanent signs. The main evacuation information never changed, but the lower panel carried seasonal messages such as ‘From this point: 6 minutes on foot to Hill Park’ or short questions like ‘If an earthquake happened now, which way would you go?’ Schools and local businesses helped rotate the messages every few months.

The town also marked several routes on the pavement. This helped people who knew they should move inland but were unsure which narrow street led most directly upward. However, officials avoided painting arrows everywhere. Too many markings could produce another form of visual overload. They focused on intersections where people had hesitated during drills.

A year later, another exercise showed better recall of specific evacuation points. The town could not prove that the changing panels alone caused the improvement because schools had also increased disaster lessons. Officials therefore avoided claiming a single solution. Instead, they continued the combination of stable core signs, changing reminders, route markings, and repeated practice.

The project illustrated a difficult principle of safety communication. Important information must be consistent enough to trust, yet familiar information can become easy to ignore. Emergency messages face an additional challenge: they describe events that people hope never to experience. If communication relies only on fear, people may avoid thinking about it. If it becomes part of the background, they may forget details.

The town's goal became not simply to make signs more noticeable, but to keep evacuation knowledge active. Permanent signs provided reliable reference points. Changing questions encouraged residents to mentally rehearse a decision. Drills connected the information to movement through real streets. None of these measures guaranteed perfect behavior in an actual disaster, when fear and damage could change conditions. But together they made the safety system less dependent on a person suddenly noticing a sign that had been invisible to their attention for years.
translation:
海沿いの町では、安全対策の見直し後、津波避難の大きな標識を設置しました。最初の一年は住民もよく話題にし、訪問者も立ち止まって読みました。しかし五年後の訓練で、多くの住民は高台の方向は知っていても、最寄りの指定避難場所を正確に思い出せないことが分かりました。

標識が古くなったのかと思われましたが、実際には清潔で読みやすく、一部は新しく交換されていました。専門家は『物理的に見えること』と『注意を向けること』は別だと指摘しました。毎日同じ標識を通ると、広告と同じように意識しなくなることがあります。

訓練後の調査では、標識を見た記憶はあっても地図や避難場所名を説明できる人は少なく、長期住民より訪問者の方が細部を覚えている場合もありました。

毎年デザインを変えるのではなく、恒久標識の下に交換可能な小パネルを追加しました。中心情報は変えず、『ここから丘公園まで徒歩六分』『今地震が起きたらどちらへ進む？』などの短いメッセージだけを季節ごとに変えました。

さらに、迷いやすい交差点だけ道路上に経路表示を付けました。矢印を増やしすぎると逆に情報過多になるため、訓練で迷いが多かった場所に絞りました。

一年後の訓練では避難場所の記憶が改善しましたが、学校教育も増えていたため、町は小パネルだけの効果とは断定しませんでした。固定標識、変化する注意喚起、路面表示、反復訓練を組み合わせて続けました。

安全情報には、信頼できる一貫性が必要な一方、慣れすぎると見えなくなるという難しさがあります。町は『標識を目立たせる』だけでなく、『避難知識を頭の中で生きた状態に保つ』ことを目標にしました。実際の災害を完全に予測することはできませんが、長年見慣れて意識から消えた標識に突然頼るより、日頃から判断を練習する方が安全につながります。
